newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori says sides closer in Peru crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori says sides closer in Peru crisis talks.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said government negotiators and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages were edging closer but had not yet agreed on an agenda for final negotiations to end the 74-day crisis, a newspaper reported on Saturday.

"What we have is a rapprochement and the differences are fewer all the time," daily El Comercio quoted Fujimori as saying during a trip on Friday to inspect flood damage in the southern Andean city of Arequipa.

But he added government negotiators and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas have yet to agree on the items that would be discussed in definitive negotiations to end Latin America's longest hostage siege without bloodshed.

The comments, reportedly made at La Joya air force base near Arequipa, were Fujimori's first since a seventh round of preliminary face-to-face talks on Thursday left mediators upbeat that progress was being made. An eighth round has been set for Monday.

With both sides bound to secrecy, details of the talks have been scarce. But mediators were upbeat on Thurdsay, saying they "noted and appreciated the desire of the participants to achieve a solution."
About 15 guerrillas have held 72 mostly middle-aged men captive at the diplomatic compound in Lima since Dec. 17, when they stormed the mansion in a flurry of explosions and gunfire.
No one was injured in the assault and rebels, who initially took hundreds of party guests hostage, have freed all but the most-prized bargaining chips.
They are demanding freedom for some 400 jailed comrades, something the government has flatly rejected.
Among the captives are Fujimori's brother Pedro, two government ministers, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
